title: A hymn in Sri Rag
hookLine: the four watches of the night picture a life from birth to old age (Sri Rag M1, ang 74)

cards: Vanjaariaa mitraa. O merchant friend. Those words run through a hymn of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, on ang seventy-four: they open every stanza and come again inside it, so a singer keeps returning to them.

Earlier on the path you read this hymn closely, the four watches of the night laid over a single life. Today the same hymn, heard the way it was written to be heard: sung, slowly, in yesterday's grave evening raga.

teach.b: On the page, the hymn is a map. In the first watch of the night, by command a life is placed in the womb. In the second, the child is carried and adored.
In the third, the mind turns to wealth and youth. In the fourth, the reaper comes to the field. Each stanza closes with Guru Nanak's name and a word to the mortal in that watch.
Now hear it in Sri Rag.

teach.h: THE TUNE HOLDS STEADY AS LIFE MOVES.
teach.b: The raga is slow and grave, and its mood holds from stanza to stanza while the life inside it moves: womb, childhood, the busy middle, the last cold stretch.
A whole night goes by in a few minutes of singing, and the music never hurries.
That steadiness does something the page can't: it makes the listener sit through each watch at the same pace, the bright ones and the hard ones alike.

teach.h: THE CALL RETURNS IN EVERY STANZA.
teach.b: And in every stanza the call comes back. Merchant friend. A trader is someone sent out with capital, expected to come back with something to show.
A friend is someone who tells you the truth while there's still time to act on it. Sung again and again, the call stops being a label and becomes a voice at the door, knocking in each watch.

So the question the hymn leaves is quieter and more present than which watch a life is in. Right now, in this hour, which watch is it? Tomorrow the music changes, to a raga from the Punjab's own soil.

how: Guru Nanak's pehre are sung in Sri Rag in kirtan, and Sikhs also read them in the Guru Granth Sahib as a reflection on the stages of a life.

games.q: what does “a hymn in sri rag” mean?
o: a hymn for the four daily times of prayer
Guru Nanak's four watches, sung in a slow raga
a ballad about traders crossing a desert

games.q: the hymn, sung — tap the pairs.
p: the reaper comes to the field
holds steady as the life moves

s: the hymn is about one actual night
the four watches of the night picture a whole life, from womb to old age.
the call to the merchant friend comes back in every stanza
so in singing it returns in every watch.
the tune speeds up as the life in the hymn speeds up
Sri Rag stays slow and steady while the life inside it moves.

games.q: a friend on the road at night calls you 'merchant'. why would the hymn picture a person as a trader?
o: because it's about trade routes in Punjab.
because a life is like capital, sent out to come back with something.
because the listeners were all merchants.
games.why: a trader is sent out with capital and expected to return with something to show; the hymn asks what a life is being traded for, watch by watch.

practice: If you can find this hymn, the pehre of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, let it play while you sit; if not, say the call softly once, vanjaariaa mitraa, and sit in the quiet it leaves.
Don't add up your whole life; just ask about this hour, whether it's a beginning, a being-carried, a building or a settling of accounts, and let the answer be small and honest.
If you pray, answer the friend's call with one Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Sri Rag. Guru Nanak's four watches of the night, sung in a slow, grave raga that holds steady while a life moves through it, with the merchant friend called in every stanza. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: O merchant friend, the call that returns in every stanza of Guru Nanak's pehre in Sri Rag.

carryVoice: Your line: which watch now. The merchant friend is called again in every stanza. Rest well.
